title: Confirmation
hookLine: many Reform communities hold confirmation at Shavuot
last: TORAH CAN BE LEARNED AT ANY AGE.

lines: TEENAGERS IN FRONT OF THE ARK.
cards: A row of teenagers stands in front of the ark, a little dressed up, a little nervous. Their bar and bat mitzvahs are behind them.

Since then they kept coming to a class, arguing about God, justice, and what they actually think. Now, on the holiday of Shavuot, each one stands up and speaks in front of their families and the whole congregation.
In many Reform communities this is called confirmation. Why this holiday? And why a second ceremony after the one at thirteen?

teach.b: You met Shavuot in your first year, and Ruth's road in your second. Today they meet a class of teenagers. Jewish tradition links Shavuot to the giving of the Torah at Sinai.
In Exodus, when Moses brings God's words down, the people answer together that they will do all of it. So a confirmation class stands, in a way, where that crowd stood: as a group, saying yes.
A few chapters later the people say it again. In the old Jewish Publication Society translation: "All that the LORD hath spoken will we do, and obey."

teach.h: WE WILL DO, AND WE WILL HEAR.
teach.b: In Hebrew, na'aseh v'nishma: we will do, and we will hear. The Talmud tells of a heavenly voice praising Israel for promising the doing before the hearing.
Some readers take it as a picture of how commitment grows: you start living it, and understanding comes along the way.

teach.h: THE FIRST YES, THEN THE SECOND.
teach.b: Then, why again? At bar or bat mitzvah, the tradition tells a young person: you are now responsible. Confirmation lets an older teenager answer back, in their own words, about what they plan to do with that.
The first yes is received. The second is chosen. And on this holiday, synagogues read the book of Ruth.
Ruth isn't born into the people she joins.
She chooses them, out loud, on a road: "whither thou goest, I will go." Sinai's yes and Ruth's yes sit side by side.
Confirmed isn't the end of learning. It's a promise made a second time, once you know a little more of what it costs.

how: In many Reform congregations, teenagers who have continued studying after bar or bat mitzvah are confirmed as a class on Shavuot, the holiday that remembers the giving of the Torah, often speaking or leading parts of the service.

games.q: you're in the crowd at Sinai. Moses reads the book of the covenant aloud. what does the crowd answer?
o: let us understand it all first, then we'll decide.
we will do, and we will hear.
we'll do the parts we like.
games.why: they promise the doing first, and the Talmud tells of a heavenly voice praising them for that order.

practice: Bring to mind one thing you said yes to before you knew everything it would ask: a friendship, a practice, a job, a promise to yourself.
Look at it as it is today, and if something in it is still worth choosing, say yes to it again, quietly, the way the class does on Shavuot.
If you pray, you can carry the words from Sinai into the quiet: we will do, and we will hear.

wordCard.voice: Confirmation: a second yes, said at Shavuot. And a week closes: the firstborn redeemed, the first haircut, honey on the letters, coming of age, teaching at thirteen, never too late, and confirmed. Today's word.

carryVoice: Your line: confirmed. A promise can be made twice, and mean more the second time. See you tomorrow.
